passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it operates precisely where the formal requirements of a binding contract have not been met, yet courts have long recognized that permitting a promisor to revoke a promise upon which another party has relied to their detriment would produce a manifest injustice. The doctrine, as it has developed through Anglo-American jurisprudence over the better part of the twentieth century, holds that where a party makes a clear and unambiguous promise, where that promise is reasonably relied upon by the promisee, and where the promisee suffers a concrete detriment as a consequence of that reliance, the promisor may be held to the promise notwithstanding the absence of consideration. Yet the precise scope of this remedy remains deeply contested, particularly with respect to the measure of relief a court ought to award and the degree to which proof of reliance should suffice in the place of a fully negotiated bargain.

The tension is perhaps most visible in the divergence between two lines of judicial authority that emerged in North American courts during the latter half of the twentieth century. One line, traceable to a series of appellate decisions in the northeastern United States during the 1960s and 1970s, holds that the appropriate remedy in a promissory estoppel case is the full expectation interest — that is, the benefit the promisee would have received had the promise been performed. Proponents of this approach argue that awarding anything less than the expectation interest degrades the promisee's reasonable anticipation and effectively penalizes prudent reliance. The competing line of authority, exemplified by a 1978 appellate ruling in a Canadian commercial dispute, awards only the reliance interest — the out-of-pocket losses actually incurred in relying on the promise — on the theory that promissory estoppel is a shield against unconscionable conduct rather than a sword by which the promisee may extract a full contractual windfall.

Furthermore, courts have struggled to articulate a principled boundary between cases in which reliance is sufficiently definite to warrant enforcement and cases in which it is merely incidental or speculative. A business that, in anticipation of a promised long-term supply contract, terminates a pre-existing supplier arrangement and retains new warehouse space presents the clearest case for relief; the reliance is both tangible and specific. But consider a party that, on the strength of a preliminary letter of intent from a prospective employer, declines to pursue several other employment opportunities. Here, the lost opportunities are genuine yet difficult to quantify, and courts have split over whether the indefinite nature of the foregone alternatives precludes a finding of actionable reliance. Regrettably, the lack of a consistent doctrinal standard has left commercial actors without reliable guidance, and legal practitioners in jurisdictions that straddle both lines of authority must counsel clients against a background of persistent uncertainty. One might reasonably hope that a systematic restatement of the reliance-interest principle would bring greater coherence to this area of the law.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was developed by courts specifically to replace the consideration requirement in all contract disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The divergence between the expectation-interest and reliance-interest remedies in promissory estoppel cases has produced a clear injustice to commercial parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel addresses genuine injustice arising from detrimental reliance, the doctrine remains incoherent in its application because courts have failed to agree on the appropriate remedy and the standard for actionable reliance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reliance-interest remedy is superior to the expectation-interest remedy because it correctly characterizes promissory estoppel as a defensive rather than an offensive doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: North American courts should abandon promissory estoppel altogether and require parties to formalize preliminary agreements through fully negotiated contracts.

explanations.correct: The passage as a whole argues that promissory estoppel addresses a real injustice but is plagued by two unresolved controversies: the measure of remedy and the definition of actionable reliance. C captures both strands and the author's overall evaluative stance.
explanations.A: Too broad and inaccurate — the passage explicitly states that promissory estoppel applies where formal contract requirements are not met, but it does not claim the doctrine was meant to replace consideration in all disputes.
explanations.B: Partly accurate but overstates the author's conclusion; the passage identifies uncertainty and lack of guidance, not a demonstrated clear injustice resulting from the split.
explanations.C: Correct — integrates the doctrinal purpose (addressing detrimental reliance) with both contested issues (remedy measure and reliance standard) and matches the author's closing call for coherence.
explanations.D: Presents one side of the judicial split as the author's own conclusion; the author presents both lines of authority without endorsing either.
explanations.E: A position nowhere advanced in the passage; the author seeks better doctrinal coherence, not abolition of the doctrine.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins traced; two competing lines of judicial authority are contrasted; one line is endorsed as superior; a recommendation is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine and the problem it addresses are introduced; two contested aspects of the doctrine are examined in turn; the author concludes by noting the practical consequences of the unresolved controversy and calling for greater consistency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal controversy is introduced; a landmark case is analyzed; the analysis is extended to related doctrines; an analogy to tort law is drawn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing doctrines are introduced simultaneously; their historical development is compared; a synthesis of the two is proposed and defended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A doctrinal tension is described; a single authoritative case resolves the tension; the implications of the resolution are explored in subsequent paragraphs.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its foundational tension; paragraph 2 examines the remedy-measure dispute (expectation vs. reliance interest); paragraph 3 examines the actionable-reliance standard, concludes with practical consequences of the split, and calls for systematic restatement. B tracks this sequence accurately.
explanations.A: Inaccurate at the end — the author does not endorse one line of authority as superior; both are presented without a declared winner.
explanations.C: No single landmark case is analyzed as central to the passage's argument, and no analogy to tort law is drawn.
explanations.D: The passage does not introduce two doctrines simultaneously, nor does it propose a synthesis of the competing remedial approaches.
explanations.E: No case resolves the tension; the passage emphasizes that the tension remains unresolved across the three paragraphs.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a condition that courts applying promissory estoppel require before holding a promisor to an unkept promise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisor must have received some benefit from the promisee's reliance, even if no formal consideration was exchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisee must demonstrate that the promise was relied upon and that the reliance resulted in concrete detriment to the promisee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promise must have been made in the context of a formally negotiated commercial transaction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The promisee must prove that the promisor acted with the specific intent to deceive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promisee must show that all other available legal remedies have been exhausted before invoking promissory estoppel.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 explicitly states three conditions: a clear and unambiguous promise, reasonable reliance by the promisee, and concrete detriment as a result of that reliance. B accurately paraphrases two of these explicitly stated elements.
explanations.A: The passage says consideration is absent, not that some benefit to the promisor is required; this inverts the doctrine's premise.
explanations.B: Correct — directly paraphrases the reliance-and-detriment elements stated in paragraph 1.
explanations.C: The passage does not limit the doctrine to formally negotiated commercial transactions; it applies precisely where formal contract requirements have not been met.
explanations.D: Deceptive intent is not mentioned as a condition; the doctrine concerns detrimental reliance, not fraud.
explanations.E: No exhaustion requirement is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that the line of judicial authority traceable to northeastern United States appellate decisions from the 1960s and 1970s holds that promissory estoppel plaintiffs should receive which of the following as a remedy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compensation limited to the actual out-of-pocket costs incurred in reliance on the promise

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nominal damages intended to acknowledge the promisor's breach without compensating for losses

choices.label: C
choices.text: The full expectation interest — the benefit the promisee would have received had the promise been performed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Equitable relief in the form of specific performance compelling the promisor to fulfill the original promise

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court-determined sum calculated by averaging the expectation interest and the reliance interest

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states explicitly that this line of authority 'holds that the appropriate remedy in a promissory estoppel case is the full expectation interest — that is, the benefit the promisee would have received had the promise been performed.' C is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: This describes the competing Canadian line of authority that awards only the reliance interest, not the northeastern U.S. line.
explanations.B: Nominal damages are not mentioned in the passage at all.
explanations.D: Specific performance is not mentioned in the passage as a remedy in either line of authority.
explanations.E: No averaging formula appears in the passage; this is a fabricated remedy.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Commercial parties would benefit from a uniform doctrinal standard clarifying when reliance is actionable and what remedy follows.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts should eliminate the reliance-interest remedy entirely because it fails to deter unconscionable conduct by promisors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The requirement of consideration should be abolished in all contract disputes so that promissory estoppel becomes the default theory of enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1978 Canadian appellate ruling correctly resolved the dispute between the expectation-interest and reliance-interest approaches.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employers who issue letters of intent should be held to the full expectation interest because preliminary employment promises are among the clearest cases for promissory estoppel relief.

explanations.correct: The closing sentence of the passage states that 'one might reasonably hope that a systematic restatement of the reliance-interest principle would bring greater coherence,' and the penultimate sentence notes that the lack of consistent doctrine leaves commercial actors without reliable guidance. A captures the inference that flows directly from both observations.
explanations.A: Correct — the author explicitly laments the lack of consistent doctrinal standards and calls for restatement to provide coherence, which entails agreement that commercial parties would benefit from such uniformity.
explanations.B: The author does not argue for eliminating the reliance-interest remedy; rather, the author seems to view it as the principle around which a restatement might be organized.
explanations.C: The passage never proposes abolishing consideration or making promissory estoppel the default enforcement theory; this overreaches the author's position.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse the 1978 Canadian ruling; it is cited as one example of a line of authority without editorial approval.
explanations.E: The author treats the employment letter-of-intent scenario as a harder case where courts have split, not a clear case for full expectation relief.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the business that terminates a pre-existing supplier arrangement and retains new warehouse space serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a scenario in which reliance is sufficiently tangible and specific to present a strong case for promissory estoppel relief

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that the expectation-interest remedy is more appropriate than the reliance-interest remedy in commercial supply disputes

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that courts consistently award relief in commercial supply cases while denying it in employment cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: concede that some forms of reliance are too speculative to warrant any judicial remedy under promissory estoppel

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide a historical example of a case in which a Canadian appellate court first applied the reliance-interest standard

explanations.correct: The author introduces the warehouse example immediately after raising the question of how courts distinguish definite reliance from incidental or speculative reliance, and describes it as 'the clearest case for relief' because 'the reliance is both tangible and specific.' Its function is to anchor one end of the spectrum before presenting the harder employment case.
explanations.A: Correct — the example is explicitly offered as the clearest case, functioning to illustrate what sufficiently definite reliance looks like.
explanations.B: The example is about the definiteness of reliance, not about which remedy measure is preferable; no comparison of expectation vs. reliance interest is made here.
explanations.C: The author says courts have 'split' on the employment scenario; no consistent pattern is demonstrated.
explanations.D: The warehouse example illustrates strong, non-speculative reliance — the opposite of what this choice states.
explanations.E: The warehouse example is a hypothetical, not a historical case, and no connection to the Canadian appellate ruling is drawn.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic approval of the doctrine's flexibility and its capacity to do justice in cases where formal contract law falls short

choices.label: B
choices.text: unqualified skepticism about whether promissory estoppel can ever provide adequate relief to parties who have relied on unkept promises

choices.label: C
choices.text: measured concern about the doctrine's lack of coherence, tempered by an underlying endorsement of its purpose and a desire for systematic reform

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral exposition of competing judicial approaches without any indication of the author's own evaluative stance

choices.label: E
choices.text: strong condemnation of North American courts for failing to adopt a uniform remedial standard despite decades of litigation

explanations.correct: The author opens by acknowledging that the doctrine addresses 'manifest injustice,' endorses its purpose, and then spends two paragraphs identifying serious doctrinal inconsistencies. The closing word 'regrettably' and the hope for 'greater coherence' signal measured concern paired with a desire for reform rather than either enthusiasm or hostility.
explanations.A: Overstates the positive valence; the author does not express enthusiasm and devotes most of the passage to cataloguing the doctrine's deficiencies.
explanations.B: Too negative — the author accepts the doctrine's validity and purpose, criticizing only its inconsistent application.
explanations.C: Correct — captures both the critical concern (incoherence, practical uncertainty) and the endorsement of the doctrine's underlying purpose.
explanations.D: Inaccurate — the author clearly editorializes with 'manifest injustice,' 'regrettably,' and the hope for systematic restatement.
explanations.E: Overstates the negative; 'strong condemnation' is too intense for an author who merely notes the lack of guidance with the word 'regrettably' and expresses hope for reform.
